records.title: The Legend of Roro Jonggrang and Prambanan Temple
records.summary: Following the defeat and death of King Boko in Central Java, the victorious prince Bandung Bondowoso sought to marry the fallen king's beautiful daughter, Princess Roro Jonggrang. Unwilling to marry the slayer of her father but unable to refuse outright, the princess set an impossible condition: he must build one thousand stone temples (candi) in a single night before dawn. Summoning legions of subterranean earth spirits (genies), Bondowoso nearly completed nine hundred and ninety-nine temples before midnight. Desperate, Roro Jonggrang ordered village maidens to pound rice in mortar bowls and light bonfires to mimic sunrise, fooling the roosters into crowing. Realizing he had been tricked with only one temple left to finish, Bondowoso cursed the princess: she turned into stone, becoming the central statue of Durga Mahisasuramardini in Prambanan Temple.
records.historical_period: Mataram Kingdom Era (9th Century CE monument, oral tradition documented 18th Century)
records.region_or_community: Sleman, Yogyakarta and Klaten, Central Java

records.title: The Legend of Lake Toba and the Goldfish Maiden
records.summary: A humble, solitary Batak farmer named Toba catches a dazzling golden fish in a mountain stream, which magically transforms into an exquisite woman. The maiden agrees to marry him under one inviolable taboo: he must never speak of her fish origin, nor insult their future offspring as a 'child of a fish.' They live happily and raise a son named Samosir. One day, Samosir is tasked with delivering lunch to his father working in the rice fields, but the hungry boy eats the food en route. Furious with hunger, Toba strikes his son, shouting: 'You cursed child of a fish!' Weeping, Samosir flees to his mother. Horrified that the sacred oath has been broken, the woman commands her son to climb the highest hill as torrential rains burst from the earth, submerging the valley into colossal Lake Toba, with Samosir Island rising at its center.
alternate_names: The Origin of Lake Toba and Samosir

records.title: Malin Kundang: The Rebellious Son Turned to Stone
records.summary: Preeminent in Minangkabau folklore of West Sumatra, Malin Kundang was an impoverished village boy raised by a loving widowed mother in Air Manis beach near Padang. Leaving home on a merchant ship to seek his fortune (merantau), Malin becomes a fabulously wealthy maritime captain with a fleet of trading galleons and a noble bride. Years later, when his flagship anchors at Air Manis, his frail, tattered mother rushes through the surf to embrace him. Ashamed of her poverty before his wealthy wife, Malin kicks his mother to the sand and spits: 'I do not have a beggar for a mother!' Weeping in anguish, the mother prays to God to judge her rebellious son. Immediately, a violent tempest shatters his ship against the beach, and Malin Kundang is turned into a stone figure kneeling in eternal regret.
alternate_names: The Cursed Son of Air Manis
geographic_associations: Air Manis Beach, Padang, West Sumatra

records.title: Sangkuriang and the Creation of Mount Tangkuban Perahu
records.summary: A defining Sundanese mythological epic of West Java, Dayang Sumbi was an ageless celestial princess exiled on earth who unknowingly raised her own son, Sangkuriang. After an adolescent quarrel, Sangkuriang left home and wandered for decades, growing into a formidable warrior. Returning to the forest, he fell passionately in love with Dayang Sumbi, neither recognizing the other. However, noticing a familiar scar on his head while combing his hair, Dayang Sumbi realized he was her biological son. To avert incest without inciting violence, she set an impossible task: he must dam the Citarum River to create a vast lake and build a giant wooden boat in a single night. Working with legions of mountain spirits (guriang), Sangkuriang nearly completed the boat when Dayang Sumbi waved white silk banners to mimic morning light. In a furious rage, Sangkuriang kicked the giant half-finished boat, which overturned to form the volcanic mountain Tangkuban Perahu ('Upturned Boat').
records.historical_period: Ancient Sundanese Oral Tradition (Bujangga Manik manuscript c. 15th Century)
records.region_or_community: Bandung Basin and West Java (Parahyangan Highlands)

records.title: Timun Mas: The Golden Cucumber and the Giant
records.summary: Desperate for a child, an elderly Javanese widow named Mbok Srini prayed to the mountain giant Buto Ijo, who presented her with a magical cucumber seed on the condition that when the child turned seventeen, she must surrender the child for him to eat. When the plant grew, a giant golden cucumber split open to reveal a baby girl, whom the widow named Timun Mas ('Golden Cucumber'). When the girl reached seventeen, the green giant arrived with an iron cudgel demanding his meal. Mbok Srini handed Timun Mas four small pouches: cucumber seeds, sewing needles, salt, and shrimp paste (terasi). Fleeing through the jungle, Timun Mas hurled the items: the seeds sprouted into a tangled jungle of vines, the needles grew into an impenetrable bamboo forest that pierced the giant's feet, the salt created a boiling sea, and the shrimp paste formed a vast, boiling swamp of volcanic mud that engulfed Buto Ijo forever.
records.region_or_community: Central Java and East Java rural villages

records.title: The Story of Cindelaras and His Champion Cock
records.summary: In the ancient East Javanese kingdom of Janggala, King Raden Putra was deceived by a jealous, scheming concubine into banishing his virtuous, pregnant queen into the deep jungle. Sheltered by forest hermits, the queen gave birth to a noble son named Cindelaras. While playing in the forest, Cindelaras discovered an eagle dropping a bird's egg, which hatched into a magnificent fighting rooster with dazzling plumage. The rooster possessed the miraculous gift of human speech, crowing: 'Kukuruyuk! I am the cock of Cindelaras, whose home is in the jungle, whose father is King Raden Putra!' Journeying to the royal palace in Surabaya to challenge the king's champion roosters, Cindelaras's rooster defeated every opponent and revealed the wicked concubine's deceit, restoring the rightful queen to her royal throne.
records.historical_period: 11th Century Janggala Kingdom Era (compiled in classical Javanese kidung)
records.region_or_community: Surabaya, Sidoarjo, and Kahuripan, East Java

records.title: Dewi Sri: The Rice Goddess of Java and Bali
records.summary: Supreme agricultural divinity of Java, Sunda, and Bali, Dewi Sri (often syncretized with Lakshmi) is venerated as the goddess of rice, fertility, and prosperity. According to sacred Javanese mythology recorded in the Manikmaya and Tantu Pagelaran, Dewi Sri was an exceptionally radiant heavenly maiden who perished of pure virtue. From her sacred burial place sprouted humanity's essential crops: from her head grew the coconut palm, from her hands sprouted tubers and medicinal herbs, from her navel arose the sugar palm, and from her heart grew sacred rice (padi). Javanese and Balinese farmers construct ornate bamboo shrines (candi bentar and paon) in the center of rice paddies to honor Dewi Sri before every planting and harvest season.
records.historical_period: Pre-Hindu animism through Classical Hindu-Javanese Mataram and Majapahit eras
records.region_or_community: Agricultural lowlands of Java, Bali, and Lombok

records.title: Calon Arang: The Witch of Girah and the Barong Dance
records.summary: Set during the 11th-century reign of King Airlangga of Kahuripan, Calon Arang was a fearsome black-magic sorceress who dwelt in the village of Girah. Infuriated because no nobleman dared propose marriage to her beautiful daughter Ratna Manggali out of terror of her dark sorcery, Calon Arang performed blood sacrifices to the goddess Durga in the cemetery. Unleashing a devastating epidemic of black plague that wiped out half of Java, corpses filled the streets. King Airlangga summoned his holiest court sage, Mpu Bharada, who sent his disciple to marry Ratna Manggali and secretly copy Calon Arang's sacred book of black magic. Neutralizing her spells, Bharada confronted the witch in a titanic spiritual battle, purifying her soul. In Balinese sacred dance, this conflict is immortalized in the sacred Barong versus Rangda temple drama.
alternate_names: The Black Magic Witch of Girah
records.historical_period: 11th Century Kahuripan Era (text compiled 1540 CE in Lontar Calon Arang)
records.region_or_community: East Java and Bali (sacred temple drama tradition)

records.title: Kebo Iwa and the Creation of Lake Batur (Bali)
records.summary: In Balinese folklore, Kebo Iwa was a benevolent but insatiably hungry giant born to an elderly couple in Bedahulu during the ancient Kingdom of Bali. Consuming entire granaries of rice and whole roasted pigs daily, Kebo Iwa protected the island from invaders and helped villagers dig irrigation canals, build stone temples, and divert mountain springs. During a catastrophic island-wide drought, villagers agreed to feed the giant if he dug a massive deep well to find water. As Kebo Iwa dug deep into the mountain bedrock, corrupt ministers from the rival Majapahit Empire, fearing his power, dumped tons of limestone and volcanic rocks down the shaft to bury him alive. The water table erupted through the rocks, flooding the crater to create beautiful Lake Batur, while the excavated volcanic earth formed Mount Batur.

records.title: The White Crocodile of the Mahakam River
records.summary: Winding through the tropical jungles of East Kalimantan on Borneo, the immense Mahakam River is home to the legendary Buaya Putih (White Crocodile). In Kutai Kartanegara kingdom oral lore, the white crocodile is an enchanted royal prince or sacred ancestral spirit that commands all aquatic wildlife, including the rare Irrawaddy river dolphins (pesut). Riverside Dayak and Kutai communities maintain strict taboos against polluting the water or killing crocodiles; if an innocent canoeist capsizes in the dangerous whirlpools, the sacred white crocodile gently carries the victim on its scaly back to shore, punishing only corrupt miners and illegal loggers who despoil the rainforest.
records.historical_period: Pre-Colonial Kutai Kingdom Era to Living River Folklore
records.region_or_community: Mahakam River basin, Kutai Kartanegara, East Kalimantan
